nodes.label: The diet–heart hypothesis
nodes.full: From the 1950s, Keys’s diet–heart hypothesis and the AHA’s 1961 advice made saturated fat the dietary villain and set vegetable oils and margarine on the healthy side; the fights of this folio unfold inside that frame.

edges: Teicholz traces the 1977 Dietary Goals to the diet–heart hypothesis and the AHA’s earlier advice.
Teicholz argues that the advice to cut animal fat pushed Americans to vegetable oils, soybean above all.
The American Soybean Association’s campaign against tropical oils protected the soybean oil market, as Teicholz and Zuckerman tell it.
Sokolof’s advertisements and the Malaysian counter-ads were the fight’s public face.
The campaign of the 1980s met a Malaysian industry that had grown 25-fold in the previous two decades.
Teicholz ties the Danish ban and the FDA label to Willett’s 1993 paper and CSPI’s 1994 petition.
Zuckerman says the FDA’s trans-fat rules are part of why US palm imports rose 263 per cent.
Most American soybean oil of 2001 was partially hydrogenated, so the labelling rule hit it directly.
Kiple ties Malaysia’s post-1960 expansion to FELDA’s smallholder schemes and the replanting of rubber land, the source of the twenty-five-fold rise Zuckerman counts.
The 2006 seizure and the 2010 voluntary standard belong to the same American weakness in policing olive oil.
Mueller’s account of olive-oil fraud runs from the 1981 poisonings to the new markets of the 2000s.
Palm oil’s American market is one outlet of the Malaysian and Indonesian industry.
Malaysia’s production growth supplied the Indian market that grew from 30,000 tonnes to 9.2 million.
The traders and refiners of the supply chain carry the oil to India and the West.
Greenpeace and others tie suppliers of the large trading firms to the deforestation of which the 2015 fires are an example.
Zuckerman presents the biofuel mandates as a further source of demand for palm oil.
Plantation expansion, fires and the labour conditions are three parts of Zuckerman’s indictment.
Teicholz presents the Women’s Health Initiative as the first large trial of the low-fat advice that the 1977 goals and the AHA had put into policy.
The FDA’s 2013 proposal and WHO’s 2018 initiative extended the move away from partially hydrogenated oils.
The FDA’s approval of olestra on 24 January 1996 followed P&G’s decades of research and a patent extension.
The growth of the US olive-oil market is the setting of the USDA’s belated standard.
Ellis describes the 1982 moratorium as the end of a whaling industry already in decline.
Relabelled Tunisian oil and the New Jersey seizure are two ends of the same fraud: cheap oil made to look extra virgin.
A voluntary US standard and a duty-free EU loophole show how little stood between cheap oil and an extra-virgin label.
